Its exchange becomes normal, hope and courage prevail among all classes, and the nation faces the future with confidence. There is no continuous whine on the part of the manufacturers in Britain such as is put up in this House every session from year to year. And if we contrast the condition in Britain to-day with the condition in Canada what do we find? Morally we must admit that the economic policy of this land is yet subject to party expediency: and we need only peruse the Speech from the Throne and some utterances of our Prime Minister-notably in Montreal, Toronto and Hamilton-to know that our government is yet in close relationship with, or even dominated by the directors of industry and finance rather than by a sense of economic justice for the workers of this Dominion. The government is backed up in this by the official opposition, and while there may be party controversy, the contest does not hinge on economic equality for all classes alike, but as to which will dare by servility to make a old for the favour of those who may for the time being, through the concentration of wealth and industry, control the policies of trade and finance of this Dominion and the lives of the people as well.
Here I want to say that to protect an industry in any country is in the end bound to act detrimentally to the interest of the protected industry itself as well as to that ol' the consuming population. To the protected interest the cost of living goes up with the amount of protection that interest enjoys, and the consuming public is handicapped in its productive work by the same process. This feature in our economic life affects every phase of government. Protection or, as I like to call it, legalized robbery, has driven our country
The Address-Air. Evans

into a condition of debt and entanglement, from which it will take the co-operation of all classes to extricate it. Our climate is good, our soil is unexcelled. Therefore the reasonable thing to do is to remove every handicap from the one industry that asks no protection, the one class that desires no favours, so that it will be free to produce. The problem for this nation to-day, as it has been for some time, the one thing for the wage earner and the agriculturist to do is to set free the government of this country from the domination of the capitalistic and manufacturing groups and revise the industrial policy of the state.
The right hon. leader of the opposition has lately been stressing the point of bringing the old national policy up to date. But the old National Policy of 1878 has been tried and found wanting. The handwriting is on the wall, and for him and his policy it might well be written to-day:
Meighen, Meighen, tekel Upharsin.
What the hon. gentleman means by bringing the old national policy up-to-date, I do not know, except it be to raise the tariff to a point which will entirely prohibit the importation of foreign goods. Now that is what the United States intended doing by the Fordney-McCom'ber tariff, and which has proved a fallacy unprecedented, so far as importation is concerned. To-day Britain is finding it quite as easy to export to the United States millions of yards of piece-goods as she did before the tariff was raised. With the amount of tariff protection the manufacturers of any country enjoy the prices will go up equal to the level of that protection. I want here to read an extract from the Recorder and Times of Brockville, a paper published daily by the Recorder Printing Company. Hon. George P. Graham, M.P., it is said, is president of that company. The Recorder and Times has seen fit to place this article in its editorial columns and describes it as a United States indictment against protection. The paragraph which I would like to bring before the House reads as follows:
Philadelphia holds the protective principle in reverence and proclaims herself "the workshop of the world," but under the highest tariff rates the United States has ever known there is a higher percentage of unemployment in protectionist Philadelphia than there is in free trade London. Not a day passes but the daily papers record suicides of people out of employment or people unbalanced by business cares. Nearly two billion dollars' worth of recently-built modern ships (built in the United States) rust at their anchorage in the rivers and harbors of the United States, in the days of the highest tariff the country has ever had. The greater portion of the finest peach crop that Georgia has ever owned has been dumped into the river or allowed to rot on the trees because
[Mr. Evans.)
American housewives cannot afford to preserve peaches with the price of sugar what it is under the highest tariff that has ever existed. Under this high tarifF there are more idle manufacturers scattered throughout all the forty-eight states than have ever before been known. In New York there is such a lot of money that under certain conditions it may be obtained at as low a rate of interest as two per cent. Notwithstanding this, because of forced withdrawals of savings from the small banks in many sections of the country over two thousands of these banks have been obliged to close their doors. A quarter of a million families, representing a million and a quarter individuals, have been forced from their farms, while an equal number remain on their farms, entirely through the leniency of their friends.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Can the hon. gentleman
tell me what the date of that article is?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: September 27, 1924. Here is an indictment against protection, describing conditions in the very country whose policy we are exhorted by the opposition members of this House to emulate. Its ships are idle because of its trade barriers. Crime is increasing because of its economic fallacy-it would seem to be a verified fact that has often been put forward, that class privilege and crime are very closely related. The prices of all commodities are high because of the centralized control which is always a feature of protection or legalized communal robbery. A contented virile population on the land is a bulwark of morality and prosperity in any country. This is particularly true of this Dominion. But we are asked to emulate a country that has driven one and a quarter million from their farm homes by a policy which robs the agriculturist of his earnings.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Some home for the protectionist.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I must say that the mind of the protectionist advocate has always been a mystery to me. There is no accounting for it in any other way than that his intellect is clouded by the prospect of immediate gain by a policy which as it benefits one class, robs other legitimate industries, agriculture in particular, of its earning. Last session we accepted the budget at the hands of the government as an earnest determination on its part to evolve a policy of free or at least freer trade. In the Speech from the Throne our attention is now drawn to the high cost of production. But the one thing which is at the root of the whole evil is to remain as it is for the present. No, even the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) is not to mention the "death knell of protection" this year, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) states in his speeches throughout the country that the government has gone far enough; the

The Address-Mr. Evans
government is upholding the hand of the protected interests, while ominous sounds of separation are heard from both the east and the middle west of this Dominion.
I wish to take a few minutes to show something of the extent of protection the manufacturer enjoys at the expense particularly of the agriculturist, under the present system of protection which my friends to my right intend to have increased at the first opportunity. Now a cut was made in the tariff last session, but no cut in the tariff schedule as it stands can be effective in lowering the cost of living in the cities or the cost of production on the farms while the tariff act is administered as it is. While the dumping act is applied by the government to discriminate against private citizens and co-operative companies, the tariff schedule may be eliminated altogether, and the manufacturer would still have all the price-fixing power that he cares to enjoy. On the farms of Canada the agriculturist for some years past has sought to lower the cost of production by co-operative effort, but here the government steps in and says, " Thou shalt not." The politician-and I say this deliberately- is and always has been the chief link in the whole chain of privilege, and the seething discontent of the Maritimes and the middle west to-day lies at the door of the government. Nor is this dumping act all in which the politician becomes the vendor of privilege. A trade discount is taken into account in computing the cost for customs purposes, amounting in the case of big deals to as high as twenty per cent. In the case of co-operative companies and individuals this is not allowed, so again the politician makes another sale of the rights of one citizen as compared with another.
In spite of the much-vaunted cut in the tariff last year, the cost of living to-day in the Dominion is quite as high or higher than it was before the paltry change was made. Goods are just as dear for the workers, the cost of production on the farms is just as high. Equality is surely one of the main attributes of government, it is an inherent quality of citizenship. Yet our citizens are classified by the government at the instigation of the manufacturing and distributing combines as to their right to import on invoice prices. As far as I can find out no such classification is mentioned in the act and the power of the board is very loosely applied. Worst of all, what makes even our parliament a nonentity and government seemingly a mercenary scramble, refunds of these sums have been made just as the importer has had the
temerity to protest or has threatened to make public the doings of the board or the secret administration of the whole act. Fair market value is interpreted, not according to the act, but according to whether the importer is a consumer, dealer, jobber or manufacturer. Sections 41 and 43 of the act are simply a nonentity as regards its administration. So is section 53 relating to the same thing. They have no definite meaning, but they are interpreted simply according to the will of the board which is guided by the mandatory instructions of those concerned. No statutory regulations seem to govern their actions. This is why I say that government in this country is simply reduced to a mercenary scramble. Our whole system of collecting revenue under the tariff is, in the way it is applied, a system of banditry as regards some of our citizens. Because of the domination of Ontario and Quebec and the means those provinces take to maintain this domination, tariff matters have become sectional in their application. Not only does the tariff act prevent competition from foreign countries against the industrial areas of Quebec and Ontario, but discriminatory freight rates as well give them protection against other parts of the Dominion. Such -are the means taken with the connivance of the government to keep up the cost of living, which is at the bottom of all our troubles. Wages, freight rates, cost of distribution and manufacture, as well as the production of all things, hinge on the cost of living. Railway managers say that freights cannot come down until wages are lower. Railway workers say that wages -are only consistent with the cost of living and that they must be left at their present level to meet the high cost. All the time our farmers are leaving the land. But the government to-day is seemingly more careful to replace us by immigration than to retain experienced farmers. Given our freedom on the land to-day, in five years time we could fill up the waste places of this Dominion with contented home makers who would set the Dominion humming with industry.
The Prime Minister stated that the leader of the opposition must know that his panacea for the ills of the nation is futile in face of the results of the by-elections of this year. But what of that? The government to-day is maintaining the same old ruinous policy that the opposition maintained from 1911 to 1922, the only deviation made being the microscopic cut in the tariff at the last session of parliament. After all the severe castigation the government received* at the hands of the leader of the opposition that hon. gentle-
The Address-Mr. Evans

man must know that the condition on the farms of Canada to-day and the closing of the 2,000 factories, which, he says, he can vouch for, is the result of his own policy. The Libby-Owens incident was brought very forcibly to the attention of this House last year. It is a tragedy in industry to-day, and I am mentioning this one case only because 1 know something of it. The Libby-Owens factory is closed because of the quality of its goods. In Saskatoon at the present time we are build'ing a sanatorium for the treatment of tuberculosis and a great deal of glass is being used in the three large sun rooms that run the whole length of the building. Up there one day, talking not long ago to the foreman, and noticing that all these glass cases came from Great Britain, I said to him: " Why did you not buy this material in Canada? Why did you not buy the Libby-Owens products?" " Oh," he said, " we could not use the stuff. It is too brittle." That is only one case where our manufacturers are lying down on the quality of the goods today and depending upon protection to carry them through.
But to return, there is no difference between the two parties; they are both championing the great communism of pelf. The policies of the two are equal. I see the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond), the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) and the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler). They are quite comfortable in the seats of the Liberals at this time, and I say that there is no difference between the two parties. Und'er present conditions agriculture is bound to languish and die, and no system of immigration will suffice to give us an increase in population under such circumstances. Under normal conditions before the war it was estimated that one out of every seven persons brought into this country and settled on the land stayed and made good. This estimate was made by two cf the most observant men in western Canada, Sir James Aikens and Mr. J. B. Mussel-man. Under this system of class privilege, however, not more than one in twelve at present can be expected to make good. I do not want to be misund'erstood in this matter: I am not opposed to immigration; I hope I shall live to see the day when the Dominion will have twenty millions of people. But we must do first things first, and the first thing to do is to set the agriculturist free, as free as God ever intended him to be.
The futility of a tariff-fed industry is amply exemplified to-day in the case of the British Empire" Steel Corporation. I have

no hesitation in naming that company. From the days of the inauguration of the Dominion Iron & Steel Company, that concern has been a source of expense and trouble to the taxpayers of the country. In bounties it has received at the hands of the taxpayer $8,115,399.75, while in remission of duties it has received nearly three quarters of a million. It received in 1921-22 as compensation for loss of contract $4,500,000. In other words, it has benefited to the extent of $13,276,672. This concern during the time of its operation has received for services, from the departments of this government, Railways and Canals, Marine and Fisheries, and Militia, no less a sum than $77,138,459. The price of rails charged to this government was $32 per ton, with $7 a ton bounty added, making a total of $39 per ton, while the same company could cut prices against the whole world to $24, delivered. This country at the time of the building of the Transcontinental railway bought its rails at $15 per ton more than it would have paid if it had brought them in from outside, and the taxpayer to-day has to meet the difference. Then we wonder why there is a deficit every year on our railways. Conditions prevail to-day at this company's works which are a disgrace to Canada and a disgrace to the name it bears. Twice since this parliament has been elected the militia has been sent in there to preserve order.

Why a dumping
duty?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I will answer the hon.
gentleman's question, and my authority is a statement made by the Minister of Customs on the floor of the House last session in answer to a question by the member for Macleod (Mr. Coote).
Fair market value is not interpreted according to the Act, but according to whether the importer is a consumer, dealer, jobber, or manufacturer. Under this legislation no consumer, no co-operative company can get the standing of dealers or distributors of agricultural implements or any other commodity; they may import. This is tyranny. And yet the agriculturists of this country are expected to operate under it. Is it right?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I do not quite understand my hon. friend. Does he say that no co-operative or private concern can import an article direct from the manufacturer in the United States?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You have it right, sir.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Who is to blame for that? Surely he is not blaming the Canadian industrialist for that. The blame must rest
upon the manufacturer of agricultural implements on the other side.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No, not at all. Why do
you put that construction upon it? It is so because the manufacturer in this country maintains that he only has a right to sell goods in this country. That is the idea of protection. The Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) made the statement in the House last session, in answer to the member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). It is true enough.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend is referring to the application of the dumping clause as passed two years ago, under which the matter is in the hands of the Minister of Customs. He supported and we opposed it.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not at all; it was passed fifteen years ago.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No, it was amended two
years ago.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman
is wrong, Mr. Speaker. The amendment to the act passed in 1922 related only to natural products. The right hon. leader of the opposition at that time gave the government the worst castigation that I have ever heard.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It was not bad enough.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I admit, Sir, it was not bad enough. But this is what I want to tell the House to-day, when I make the point that there is no difference between the two parties: both the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) and the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) voted with the government.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: On what?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
On that amendment. There is no mistake; I took a note of it at the time. I see it is six o'clock, Mr. Speaker. I hope I have been able to bring before you the conditions under which agriculture is labouring to-day. Agriculture must have these conditions removed before the present population, or any augmented population, can operate successfully.
At six o'clock the House adjourned without question being put, pursuant to rule.
The Address-Mr. Evans

Thursday, February 12, 1925
